title: How the bare nails trend became a class issue
content:
In recent months, Paloma Buddemeier has watched a stream of people walk into her nail salon with the goal of looking as if they'd never been there at all.
"It's crazy," the owner of Wumman Spa in London says.
These customers still get their nails filed, buffed, and trimmed. "You still do the cuticle, you do the soaking and hydrate everything," says Buddemeier, "but you just put no polish on."
Driving this, she says, is a viral craze for bare-looking nails.
In recent months, artsy shots of glossy naked nails have been flooding social media and taking over fashion runways and red carpets, which some are viewing as the latest symbol of "quiet luxury".
But critics argue the bare nails trend actually says something about class, the hamster wheel of beauty standards, and who gets to define what is considered tasteful.
Nail art's historical and creative roots are linked back to black, Latino, and Asian communities and the suggestion that bare nails are now a sign of high status could stigmatise bold manicures, they say.
"That trend really promotes blankness and this kind of sameness and erasure of culture and identity that is so important to black and brown communities," beauty journalist Kristina Rodulfo tells the BBC.
"They are often called elegant or tasteful, and these are often usually euphemisms that perpetuate white supremacist standards of beauty."
For some, though, the choice is less about a dislike of bold nails and more about simplifying their routine.
Some converts say they're ditching polish as a way of rebelling against an entrenched female beauty standard or to save time and money. Others just love the look. Then, there are some women who've long left their nails alone, amused to find their routine – or lack thereof – suddenly in vogue.
For years, Irish TV presenter Angela Scanlon marched herself to a nail salon every fortnight, a routine that started when she was living in New York in the 2000s. There, she says, manicures were so universal they felt like a uniform. But it soon became a chore.
Scanlon would have everything from thin, shiny shellac to sturdier "Builder In A Bottle" gel manicures layered onto her nails every other week without fail.
"It wasn't like I was in my head going: 'I must go because Dave from Hull is going to be disgusted if I'm on This Morning next week without a full set'," the Radio 2 presenter says. "I just added it to the list of things that we must do... in the way you would wash your hair."
Eventually, in a moment of clarity, Scanlon decided to stop going, in a bid to free up time and mental bandwidth.
"I heard myself saying to people: 'Ugh, my god, I have to go and get my nails done.'
"And I thought: 'I probably don't need to do this anymore'."
Scanlon's posts about her decision to ditch the continuous manicure blew up on Substack and Instagram earlier this year. She seemed to have tapped into a vein.
Simple nails were in the spotlight at New York Fashion Week in February, with Marc Jacobs among those sending his models out polish-less, though some fashionistas argue this is not new.

title: What is kratom, the 'gas station heroin' alarming officials in the US?
content:
Jeffrey Deaver, a 58-year-old retired timber cutter in the state of Washington, has taken kratom for four years to help with severe chronic hip and knee pain.
He discovered the herbal product when he couldn't find relief from doctors and while waiting for surgeries. Scared at first, he "started small", but then took more until his pain went away.
"It was like a miracle," Deaver said. "I could sleep. I could function.
"I just don't know what I'd do without it."
Kratom - a herb with opioid-like effects - has grown in popularity in the US over the last decade, and is typically purchased over the counter and consumed in pill or liquid form.
This week, investigators found packaged kratom in the possession of two deceased University of Mississippi students. Although their deaths were not attributed to kratom, officials are now issuing warnings about its consumption.
For years, anti-kratom advocates have pushed for bans, and in some countries, like the UK, it's illegal. But Kratom is not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration and is legal in some states, including Mississippi.
Here's what we know about it:
Kratom is a tree that is native to Southeast Asia in countries like Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia.
It's been used for centuries for its stimulant properties, grounded and consumed similar to tea.
As its popularity spread around the globe, it entered the US market as a supplement around 2016.
"That's really where the problems began," said Dr Shane Speights, dean of the New York Institute of Technology College of Osteopathic Medicine at Arkansas State University.
In the US kratom is mostly sold in highly concentrated forms either via pill, powder or liquid, Speights said.
It's also widely available - found everywhere from convenience stores and petrol stations to vape shops.
Also, because of the supplement classification, kratom products are not federally regulated.
"There's no way to know exactly what you're getting," Speight said. "You could go and create something in your basement, market it as a supplement, and nobody's really going to check and see what's in it."
Kratom is often marketed as a safe, natural herbal supplement that helps with pain management, anxiety and depression.
In lower doses, its stimulant properties create a "caffeine-kind of buzz", Speights explained.
Because of its opioid-like effects, it has also been used with the goal of curbing addictions to actual opioids like fentanyl.
Those properties stem from the way the plant's compounds - like 7-Hydroxymitragynine - activate various hormones, including dopamine.

title: 'This is fixable': What really helps save a relationship
content:
What couples therapists want you to know about trying to save a relationship that's going downhill.
If you're in an unhappy relationship, you may suffer from heartache – literally.
Vicious arguments can result in poor sleep and even heart pain and muscle pain . They can make everyone in the family, including children, more vulnerable to physical and mental health problems. A happy relationship can boost your health and even your lifespan . An unhappy one can have the opposite effect, raising your risk of an earlier death by chipping away at your health.
In fact, poor-quality close relationships are considered a health risk factor equal to or greater than smoking or lack of exercise. And then, of course, there's the metaphorical heartache: the pain of love unravelling.
So how do you turn an unhappy relationship into a happy one? And is that even possible?
A growing body of research reveals some surprising answers – and spells hope for couples committed to a turnaround.
If you enter a new relationship and the first argument you have with your partner is about dirty dishes, you may be catching a glimpse of the distant future: research suggests that what couples argue about remains pretty constant throughout the relationship. These recurring problems are known as perpetual or gridlocked issues.
"Those gridlocked issues could be about finances, parenting, their sex lives, how they negotiate power in the relationship," says Carrie Cole, a psychologist and the director of research at The Gottman Institute for couples therapy in Seattle, US. But also, they can be about seemingly minor issues such as neatness.
In one longitudinal study, psychologist John Gottman and his team observed couples' disagreements in an initial assessment, and four years later. They found that 69% of the time the couples were still arguing over the same type of issues they had debated those four years earlier.
Other studies have revealed a similar pattern, with certain core issues such as money coming up in conflicts across households and even across cultures . Disagreements over money, in particular, cause the most persistent and heated rows. Unequal division of housework is another cause of tensions, and can raise the likelihood of divorce.
In itself, disagreement isn't necessarily a bad sign. It can just be a natural part of learning to understand and respond to each other's needs . And both happy and unhappy couples argue.
The crucial difference between happy and unhappy couples is how they behave towards each other, research suggests – during and also outside of arguments.
Cole cites four specific behaviours that signal your relationship may be headed for a break-up , according to studies: criticism, contempt , defensiveness and stonewalling (which means withdrawal from a conflict by refusing to engage).
"Those four behaviours will kill a relationship," says Cole. But, she adds, "they are fixable, if the couple wants to fix them." (Read on for specific tips.)
In fact, it's not just the relationship that's at risk: separate research has shown that persistent criticism from one's partner significantly predicts an earlier death.
Arguments involving these kinds of behaviours, along with aggression and hostility, are known as destructive – and can ultimately raise the risk of divorce .
However, constructive arguments, which focus on mutually resolving issues with respect, curiosity and kindness, can strengthen your relationship.
One key factor is responsiveness: the feeling that your partner listens , supports and understands you. Experiencing your partner as responsive is not only associated with greater marital satisfaction , but can even buffer inflammation and boost physical health and longevity .
Kindness and cooperation can also build long-term goodwill. One 20-year-study of married couples showed that shared decision-making and equally shared housework were associated with greater marital happiness and lower conflict.
How couples argue may even affect their sleep : destructive arguments are associated with bad sleep, while constructive ones are associated with good sleep, research has found.

World leaders renew commitment to protect the world from future pandemics
Political leaders meeting at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) renewed their commitment to making the world safer from future pandemics, stressing the need for sustained and more equitable investment and action on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response (PPPR).
The UNGA today held its second High-level Meeting on PPPR, following its first staged in 2023 in response to the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic and gaps in global health security. Countries stressed that strengthening PPPR is not a health issue alone – it requires a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach, with involvement of communities and all relevant sectors.
Leaders recognized the progress made in the past three years to strengthen global systems to detect, prepare for and respond to pandemic threats, including adoption of the WHO Pandemic Agreement and amendments to the International Health Regulations (2005). Capacities and infrastructure for PPPR have also been scaled up with the establishment of global centres dedicated to epidemic and pandemic surveillance, sharing of pathogens, and local manufacturing of vaccines, treatments and diagnostics.
Addressing today’s meeting, WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, however, said that continued action and investment were needed to sustain progress and better prepare the world to respond to threats like COVID-19, which was linked to more than 20 million excess deaths between 2020 and 2023, and wiping over US$ 10 trillion from the global economy.
"The COVID-19 pandemic exposed and exacerbated the fault lines of global health security, and taught the world many painful lessons," said Dr Tedros. "The political commitment shown today reflects those lessons, and includes important commitments to concrete, measurable and urgent action to build and strengthen local and national capacities, to invest in resilient health systems, and to expand equitable access to products, tools and resources."
Countries also stressed the urgent need to successfully finalize negotiations on an annex to the WHO Pandemic Agreement to establish the Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) system, which is currently being negotiated by WHO Member States.
The purpose of the PABS annex is to operationalize a system for the timely sharing of pathogens with pandemic potential, and benefits arising from their use. This will enable research, development and timely and equitable sharing of vaccines, medicines, diagnostics and other health products arising from those pathogens. Adoption of the Annex at the coming World Health Assembly, in May 2027, is necessary for WHO Member States to start national consideration to ratify the WHO Pandemic Agreement.
“The Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing System, under negotiation, is critical to unlocking the full potential of the WHO Pandemic Agreement. There is no time to waste,” said Mrs Amina Mohammed, the United Nations Deputy Secretary-General, speaking on behalf of UN Secretary-General Mr António Guterres. “I call on Member States to accelerate these actions. Let’s get it done. Let’s deliver the Pandemic Agreement the world is waiting for.”
The Declaration underscores that national health security can only be achieved with global solidarity, and that international cooperation is essential for protecting communities and countries from cross-border threats.
Recognizing that preventing pandemics begins long before an outbreak, the declaration highlights the importance of a One Health approach that addresses the connections between human, animal and environmental health.
In opening the meeting, Dr. Khalilur Rahman, President of the 81st UN General Assembly, said international cooperation was essential to protect the world from inevitable future pandemics through equitable and timely access to vaccines, diagnostics, therapeutics and other essential medical supplies, stronger health systems and closing persistent financing gaps to empower people and communities.
“We have the knowledge, we have the tools, we have the science and expertise, and we have the hard lessons of COVID-19,” Dr Rahman told the meeting. “Let us use them for ourselves, our families and our loved ones. And also in memory of those we lost and in recognition of all those who suffered, needlessly.”
Ambassador Amar Bendjama, President of the UN Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC), said pandemic preparedness, prevention and response were crucial for advancing the 2030 Agenda and advancing progress across the Sustainable Development Goals.
“This calls for integrated and adequately financed action, with equity and sustained investment in resilient health systems, technology access, prevention and early warning,” Ambassador Bendjama said. “ECOSOC has a critical role to play in bringing together Member States, the United Nations system, and other stakeholders to strengthen policy coherence and coordinated action in this area.”
As discussions continued throughout the day, leaders taking part in the HLM emphasized that prevention, preparedness and response must remain a sustained political priority, not only during crises but in the years between them. They stressed that protecting the world from future pandemics will require continued political leadership, international cooperation and long-term investment.
The second United Nations General Assembly High-level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response is being held on 25 September 2026 at United Nations Headquarters in New York. The meeting is reviewing progress since the 2023 High-level Meeting and considering a Political Declaration focused on strengthening pandemic prevention, preparedness and response through equity, solidarity, multilateral cooperation and sustainable investment. The declaration is expected to be forwarded to the United Nations General Assembly for further consideration.
The overall theme of the High-level Meeting is on fostering a multilateral and intergenerational approach to prevent, prepare for and respond to pandemics and public health emergencies, through the principles of equity and solidarity.
The Meeting also includes two multi-stakeholder panels on 1) the multilateral actions needed for stronger PPPR, and 2) how to ensure equitable access to critical tools through sustainability and predictability, including capacities and financing

Recommendations announced for influenza vaccine composition for the 2027 southern hemisphere influenza season
The World Health Organization (WHO) today announced its recommendations for the viral composition of influenza (or ‘flu’) vaccines for use in the 2027 southern hemisphere influenza season. The announcement was made following an international consultation on the composition of influenza virus vaccines.
Seasonal influenza causes substantial illness and many hospitalizations each year. Regular updates to vaccine composition are needed because influenza viruses continually evolve. WHO’s recommendations are used by national vaccine regulatory agencies and pharmaceutical companies around the world to develop, produce, and license influenza vaccines for the following influenza season. This ensures that vaccines are closely matched to the viruses expected to circulate, offering the best possible protection against severe illness and death.
Twice each year, WHO convenes experts from its Collaborating Centres and Essential Regulatory Laboratories to review surveillance data generated through the Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS) and other sources, and recommend vaccine compositions for upcoming influenza seasons.
"For nearly 75 years, the WHO Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System has demonstrated the power of global solidarity in public health," said Dr Maria Van Kerhove, WHO's Director for Epidemic and Pandemic Management. "The commitment of countries and laboratories to share data, viruses and expertise enables WHO to make timely vaccine recommendations, strengthening our collective ability to detect and respond to emerging influenza threats. This is global public health collaboration at its best."
From February to August 2026, influenza A(H1N1)pdm09, A(H3N2) and influenza B viruses circulated in varying proportions across all regions of the world, causing disease. Influenza A viruses were the most common in most regions, except Northern and Western Africa, North America and Eastern Asia, where influenza B viruses dominated.
WHO recommends that vaccines for use in the 2027 southern hemisphere influenza season contain the following:
Egg-based vaccines
Cell culture-, recombinant protein- or nucleic acid-based vaccines
As part of the review, experts also looked at influenza viruses circulating in animals, particularly those that have caused infections in humans. These animal or zoonotic influenza viruses remain a significant concern because of their potential to cause pandemics.
These biannual meetings include a detailed assessment of these viruses and the selection of new candidate vaccine viruses (CVVs) from contemporary zoonotic influenza viruses, which can be used rapidly to manufacture vaccines should a pandemic threat arise. Information on newly selected zoonotic influenza CVVs is available on the WHO website .

WHO announces expansion of prequalification programme for medical devices
The World Health Organization (WHO) today announced a major expansion of its prequalification programme to include a wider range of life-saving medical devices such as contraceptives and innovative tuberculosis (TB) screening technologies. This broadens the range of quality-assured, safe and effective products covered by the programme, which already includes in vitro diagnostics (medical tests) and male circumcision devices.
The WHO prequalification programme helps ensure that essential health products meet international quality, safety and performance standards for global procurement. Medical devices are assessed through an independent, standardized and transparent process. Products that meet the required standards are included in the WHO list of prequalified medical devices, providing trusted guidance for United Nations agencies, procurement organizations, donors and national authorities.
The expansion is particularly significant for countries with limited regulatory capacity. An estimated 70% of countries report inadequate or weak regulatory systems for medicines and vaccines, with even greater challenges for other health products. By expanding the programme, WHO will help countries improve access to quality-assured medical devices such as male and female condoms, intrauterine devices (IUDs), computer-aided detection software for tuberculosis (CAD-TB) screening and male circumcision devices.
“Everyone, everywhere, should be able to rely on medical devices that are safe, effective and meet high standards of quality,” said Dr Sylvie Briand, WHO Chief Scientist and Assistant Director-General a.i. for Health Systems, Access and Data. “By expanding WHO prequalification, we are strengthening confidence in these essential health products and helping countries expand equitable access to the technologies people need to protect and improve their health.”
A key part of the expansion is the transfer of prequalification for male and female condoms and IUDs from the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) to WHO. Access to quality-assured condoms and IUDs is essential for sexual and reproductive health. These products help prevent unintended pregnancies and support informed decisions about family planning. Condoms also play a critical role in preventing HIV and other sexually transmitted infections.
Male circumcision devices are now part of the WHO’s broader medical device prequalification framework, whereas they were previously assessed under a separate process. WHO prequalified devices support safe, standardized voluntary medical male circumcision services, which can reduce men’s risk of acquiring HIV through heterosexual exposure by approximately 60%.
The expansion also includes computer-aided detection (CAD) software for tuberculosis (TB) screening, bringing a digital health technology into the WHO prequalification programme. CAD software uses digital chest X-rays and artificial intelligence to identify people who may have TB and need further testing. This is particularly important in countries with a high TB rate, where reliable screening can help detect TB earlier and connect people to diagnosis and treatment quickly.
More information on the transition, next steps and the first assessment wave for contraceptive devices, CAD-TB products and male circumcision devices is available on the WHO website .

WHO to update the recommendations on criteria and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy
One in six live births (21 million per year) is affected by hyperglycaemia during pregnancy. Hyperglycaemia in pregnancy includes diabetes that existed before pregnancy, diabetes first diagnosed during pregnancy, or gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), a form of elevated glucose (blood sugar) levels that appears during pregnancy. Distinguishing between these conditions is often challenging, particularly in settings with a high prevalence of undiagnosed pre-existing diabetes.
Hyperglycaemia during pregnancy is associated with increased risks of adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes , including hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, stillbirth, macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycaemia, birth injury, and other long-term complications. Early identification and accurate classification of hyperglycaemia during pregnancy are therefore critical to enable appropriate care and reduce the risk of adverse outcomes.
Given the substantial and growing global burden of diabetes, with most cases occurring in low- and middle-income countries, guidance that is applicable across diverse resource settings is needed. With a view to improving maternal and newborn outcomes worldwide, the World Health Organization (WHO) published its first recommendations on care for women with diabetes during pregnancy in November 2025.
The updated recommendations set to come out in 2026 will include updates on the 2013 recommendations on the diagnostic criteria and classification of hyperglycaemia first detected during pregnancy . New evidence has emerged regarding approaches to screening, diagnosis, and classification, highlighting the need to revisit this guidance. Revising these recommendations has been prioritized as part of WHO’s broader efforts to address non-communicable diseases in pregnancy and improve maternal and newborn health outcomes worldwide.
A Guideline Development Group (GDG) meeting will be held 20–24 October 2026 to review the evidence base on the screening and diagnosis of hyperglycaemia in pregnancy. In keeping with the requirements of the WHO Compliance, Risk Management and Ethics Office, we are posting online short biographies of the GDG members . The listed candidates have also submitted a declaration of interest form stating any conflict of interests. WHO has applied its internal processes to ensure that the performance of the above tasks by members of this group will be transparent and without any significant conflict of interests (academic, financial or other) that could affect the credibility of the guideline.
Nevertheless, WHO invites the public to review the experts and stakeholders involved and provide feedback regarding any member deemed to have a significant conflict of interest with respect to the terms of reference for this group. Comments and feedback should be cordial and constructive, and sent to srhmph@who.int .
This WHO normative meeting is by invitation only.
NOTE:
The GDG members are participating in the meeting on their individual capacity. Affiliations are presented only as a reference. The participation of experts in a WHO meeting does not imply that they are endorsed or recommended by WHO nor does it create a binding relationship between the experts and WHO. The biographies have been provided by the experts themselves and are the sole responsibility of the individuals concerned. WHO is not responsible for the accuracy, veracity and completeness of the information provided. In accordance with WHO conflict of interest assessment policy, expert’s biographies are published for transparency purposes. Comments and perceptions are brought to the knowledge of WHO through the public notice and comment process.
Comments sent to WHO are treated confidentially and their receipt will be acknowledged through a generic email notification to the sender. Please send any comments to the following email: srhmph@who.int . WHO reserves the right to discuss information received through this process with the relevant expert with no attribution to the provider of such information. Upon review and assessment of the information received through this process, WHO, in its sole discretion, may take appropriate management of conflicts of interests in accordance with its policies.
